assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a tunable platform for flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity, and spawned the whole moire materials field. It is exactly the kind of quantum behaviour in materials that surprised theorists. The theory predicted the flat band and the experiments then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at the predicted angle, which is the theory-experiment loop I value.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experimental discovery. Andrei's group had independent early work on flat bands in twisted graphene and a case could be made for her, but a three-person prize is cleanest with theory plus the key experiment.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced the correlated and superconducting states, and the field has grown for years. Interpretation of the superconducting pairing is still debated, but the discovery itself is robust and timely.
uncertainties: Whether Eva Y. Andrei's contribution should displace one of the three names
Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled
Sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility details
My recollection of priority between early STM flat-band work and the 2018 transport results is not independently verified

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators established a new class of quantum matter with protected edge and surface states, grounded in band-structure theory that can be computed from first principles. It had a large impact across condensed matter, with clear links to spectroscopy (ARPES) and transport.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the quantum spin Hall idea; Molenkamp's group observed it in HgTe wells; Hasan's ARPES work established 3D topological insulators. Mele is dropped only because of the three-person limit, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) are not on the supplied list, so the credit picture is incomplete and contested. This entry overlaps with B029 and B045, so the topological-insulator theme should be settled as one decision.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed many times in transport and ARPES, with computational material predictions, and the field is mature. Timing is reasonable given how long it has been since the discoveries.
uncertainties: Priority disputes among Kane/Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and others, and who is left out
Overlap with B029 and B045 could split support
Some early claims, such as particular ARPES surface-state interpretations, were refined later; I rely on memory here

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and then giant TMR in crystalline MgO junctions are a case where a spin-dependent tunneling effect, explained by electronic-structure theory of coherent Bloch-state filtering, became the basis of hard-disk read heads and MRAM. It combines a clear physical discovery with decades of use.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa independently demonstrated large MgO TMR in 2004, following first-principles predictions by Butler and by Mathon and Umerski, who are not credited here. Choosing three of four is a real compromise, and the credit is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, widely confirmed and in industrial use. Fairly recognized already through the 2007 GMR prize, which might make the committee wary of overlapping with a spintronics prize.
uncertainties: Whether Shinji Yuasa should rank above one of the named three
Theory contributors (Butler, Mathon-Umerski) are outside the credited names
Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may reduce the novelty argument

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fractional charge and anyonic exchange statistics are among the most striking quantum results in condensed matter: quasiparticles that are neither bosons nor fermions. The experiments recently reached direct braiding and collider-type measurements, so a long-standing theoretical concept has been put to test.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim introduced the idea of intermediate statistics in two dimensions in 1977; Heiblum's group did early shot-noise measurements of fractional charge. Fève and Manfra have done the recent anyon-statistics experiments. Five names for at most three seats, and prominent others (Wilczek, Laughlin, Halperin, Arovas-Schrieffer) are not in the list, so the allocation is awkward.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is well confirmed. Direct anyon statistics experiments are only recent (2020 onward) with a few groups and interferometry subtleties, so the recognition could be early.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among five named people and omitted theorists
Interpretation of interferometry results is still being scrutinized and independent replication is limited
Whether the prize should rather target the earlier fractional charge result

assessment.nobel_worthiness: DMFT gave the first controlled, non-perturbative treatment of strong correlations, explaining Mott transitions and, with DFT (DFT+DMFT), quantitative spectra of real correlated materials. It is a quantitative theory that connects directly to photoemission and is widely used.
assessment.attribution: Georges and Kotliar built the DMFT mapping in 1992 onto the impurity problem; Vollhardt, with Metzner, introduced the infinite-dimension limit in 1989. Metzner is not in the credited list, which weakens the fairness of any prize configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely used, but verification is partly methodological: approximations in finite dimensions and limits of impurity solvers remain. Nobel prizes for pure theory methods are less common; the physical discovery is less singular than for other candidates.
uncertainties: Metzner is missing from the credit list
Whether a method counts as a discovery in the Nobel sense
Known limitations for spatial correlations

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, using the magic-wavelength idea, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. This is a clear and verified invention with real use.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and built the first clock; Ye drove the record accuracy and many-body lattice clocks. Hall and Hansch were honored in 2005 for the comb, and Ye worked closely with Hall, so the line between the earlier recognition and this is partly blurred. A two-person prize looks fair.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories confirm the performance, and clock comparisons are ongoing. The remaining question is whether the redefinition of the second has happened yet, which may make recognition slightly early.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 prize for the optical frequency comb
Other contributors (e.g. strontium and ytterbium clock groups) could be overlooked
Outside my own area, so I defer to colleagues on priority

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models in a controlled setting, and the Mott-insulator transition and later quantum gas microscopes allow single-site observation of many-body states. It is a close cousin to the correlated-electron problems I care about, and it offers a precise test of theory.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner (with Bloch and Hansch) observed the superfluid to Mott transition in 2002; Bloch led many subsequent developments. The list has five names, and Esslinger (Fermi-Hubbard) and Cirac are plausible alternatives. Zoller also appears in other candidates, which could complicate configurations across the shortlist.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature and well replicated, though practical analog simulation beyond what classical computers can do is still an open goal. The prize for ultracold gases (2001) already exists, so the committee might ask how new this discovery is.
uncertainties: Which three of five names, and whether Esslinger belongs
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize
Whether quantum simulation has delivered a decisive new result beyond classical methods

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetic order with spin-split bands but zero net magnetization, which follows from symmetry analysis and DFT. As a magnetism theorist I find it an important conceptual advance with potential for spintronics. First-principles calculations predicted candidate materials and ARPES/XMCD experiments have begun to confirm spin splitting.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth articulated the classification around 2019-2022. Earlier related work by other groups (e.g. on momentum-dependent spin splitting in antiferromagnets) may share credit. Allocation among the three is plausible but not settled.
assessment.maturity: Premature in my view. Experimental confirmation in MnTe and CrSb is recent (2024), few independent groups have verified it, and device relevance is not shown. It is better as a future candidate than as a prize now.
uncertainties: Short time since experimental confirmation
Credit for earlier related spin-splitting predictions
Whether practical impact will follow
I may be biased because it is close to my own field
